Mini-Review on Exoplanet Detection Methods
Markus Pössel
IAU Office of Astronomy for Education, 2026
Exoplanets, connected as they are to the search for life on other planets, are an
attractive topics to students of all ages. Detecting them, however, is a challenge.
Most exoplanets have only been detected indirectly. The indirect methods are
based on concepts and phenomena that are accessible to school students, and this
mini-review gives a bare-bones account of those methods.
The methods reviewed here are the “classical” detection methods: the radial
velocity method and the transit method. Beyond the basics presented here, there
are interesting new developments afoot: With the planned fourth data release
(DR4) of the Gaia mission of the European Space Agency ESA, the astrometric detection method, where an exoplanet’s orbit is estimated from the host star’s
minute shifts in the night sky, is likely to become more important. Over the past
few years, measurements with the James Webb Space Telescope of spectra, extracted both from direct observations and from exoplanet transits, have opened
up a whole new field of atmospheric studies of exoplanets. With the upcoming
start of NASA’s Roman Space Telescope later this year, direct observations will
become more important: Roman has a coronagraph on board, which will allow
for direct observations of planets while “blotting out” the light of the central star.

Radial Velocity

The radial velocity of the star can be measured via the Doppler effect: well-defined
spectral lines of the star shift toward the red end of the spectrum when the star
moves away from us, and toward the blue end when it moves toward us. If we
were viewing the orbital plane edge-on, the radial velocity would depend only

3

Radial Velocity Method

For most exoplanetary systems, it is impossible to obtain a resolved image, that
is, an image that shows the star, the planet and their mutual separation. Instead,
we only “see” the star itself, and any deductions about the presence of a planet
need to be made from measurements on the host star only. The planet is typically
invisible with current technology (a helpful simile: the brightness ratio between
star and planet is like trying to detect a firefly next to a stadium spotlight from
several kilometers away).
In many cases, the star’s radial velocity can be detected via the Doppler effect,
as we have examined in the preceding section. In the simplest case, with only one
planet present, the radial velocity varies periodically. From this, we can determine
an important observational quantity: the orbital period P.
The radial velocity method exploits this phenomenon. By measuring the Doppler
shift, we can reconstruct the velocity curve (13) and thus determine the quantity
v∗ · sin ι.
You can interactively explore the fundamental setup in the browser-based app

The approximation in the final step is valid because planetary masses are typically

Thus, the radial velocity method provides an estimate for MP · sin ι. Since sin ι
ranges from 0 to 1, MP · sin ι sets a lower bound on the planet’s mass MP .

4

Transit Method

If by chance we see a given exoplanet system edge-on or nearly edge-on, there is
another way of indirectly detecting the planet: the transit method, which detects
planets indirectly by observing periodic changes in brightness as an observer on
Earth sees the planet pass in front of its host star.
You can interactively explore the fundamental setup and see how the transit
light curve changes as a function of the system’s fundamental parameters in the
browser-based app available under the following URL:
https://astro-apps.org/TransitMethod/index.html
The following quantitative analysis presents simplified versions of the calculations
from the paper Seager and Mallén-Ornelas 2002. The first formula relating the
parameters is straightforward: in most cases, the planet’s disk passes completely
in front of the star’s disk during a transit. In the light curve, this shows as a
nearly flat stretch near the brightness minimum, corresponding to the time when
the planet is fully in front of the star. To first approximation, assuming each
region of the stellar disk appears equally bright (which is not strictly true due to
limb darkening), the fractional decrease in flux ∆F is

In this figure, the upper part shows the view from Earth if we had an extremely
high-resolution telescope—the (brighter) stellar disk and four positions A, B, C,
and D of the planet’s disk as it moves from left to right. The lower part shows the

The times when the planet’s disk is at positions A, B, C, and D are marked. Qualitatively, the curve is straightforward: before reaching position A, the star has its
normal brightness. Starting at A, the planet begins to transit, and the brightness
decreases—by an amount exaggerated by a factor of 10 here for clarity. At position B, the planet is fully in front of the star, and the minimum brightness phase
begins. This continues until position C, after which the planet starts to move out
from behind the star, until at position D it no longer obscures any part of the star,
and the star returns to its original brightness.
